covers.quote: The academic and professional titles held by individuals usually have initial capitals. This includes honorary titles.
Use initial capitals for titles that appear immediately before a person’s name. Do this unless the title is generic.
Also use initial capitals for the shortened forms of titles.
Use initial capitals for official titles that replace a name.
Titles replacing a name also have initial capitals:
when you address someone directly
for salutations in correspondence.
Keep the initial capital for the title in correspondence when you’re writing to a specific person.

parts.quote: Our new vice-chancellor and president is Professor Rufus Black.
We welcome Dr Jamilah Mulyadi to our clinic. Dr Mulyadi is now available for skin examinations.
The Vice-Chancellor of the University of Tasmania visited last week.
‘We note your concerns Doctor. Thank you for bringing this evidence before the committee’.

rules.quote: Use initial capitals for the titles of individual academics and professionals
rules.violation_condition: A non-generic academic or professional title is written with a lower-case initial where it identifies an individual before their name, replaces their name as an official title, addresses them directly, or forms part of a full title.
when: Includes honorary titles and shortened forms of titles.
Applies to non-generic titles immediately before a name.
Applies to official titles replacing a name, direct address and correspondence salutations.
Applies to titles after a name only when they form part of a full title.
Generic titles are checked under the lower-case rule instead.
rules.why: G-2 and G-4: these are contexts and restatements of the same initial-capital check, not separate findings.

covers.quote: Use lower case if you use a title generically.
For all other uses, titles that replace a name should be lower case.

These other uses include abbreviated titles and titles given by an organisation to a role or position. Academic and professional organisations might capitalise such titles as a mark of respect or status, but this is not Australian Government style. Treat them as generic and use lower case.
Use lower case for most titles that appear after a name. These titles describe the individual and are generic.
Only use initial capitals for titles after a name in a full title.
Generic use of academic and professional titles includes:
titles that describe a named individual
plural titles
common nouns.
Some titles appearing immediately before a name are also generic because they describe the individual. These titles are usually preceded by ‘the’ or a modifier.

parts.quote: All general surgeons at the hospital attended Wednesday’s forum.
The vice-chancellor visited Burnie campus last week.
They met with Associate Professor Dianne Stephens OAM, medical director of the National Critical Care and Trauma Response Centre.
Professor Bartlett, the university’s vice-chancellor, welcomed alumni to the reception.
The research fellow Lydia Mbegngue wrote extensively on this topic.
Several postdoctoral fellows in the research facility met last week.
A provost oversees a university’s academic performance.
Dhriti Saxena is a local doctor in general practice.
They met with former medical director Tom Perera.
Two doctors from this practice attended the conference.
It is important to see your doctor to develop an asthma action plan.

rules.quote: Use lower case for titles used in a generic way
rules.violation_condition: A generic academic or professional title has an initial capital, including a descriptive title, plural title, common noun or abbreviated role title replacing a name.
when: Most titles after a name are generic; titles in a full title are the exception.
A title before a name can be generic when it describes the individual, often following ‘the’ or a modifier.
Abbreviated titles and organisation-given role titles replacing a name are generic unless an official-title, direct-address or salutation case applies.
An organisation’s preference for respectful capitals does not by itself make a generic title capitalised.
Signature blocks may follow the organisation’s template, including its prescribed all-capitals treatment.
rules.why: G-2 and G-4: generic uses before, after and instead of a name are cases of one lower-case check.

covers.quote: A full title includes the title or honorific (with initial capitals), name, post-nominals, position and organisation.
Use a full title:
to introduce an individual as speaker
in address and signature blocks in correspondence
in official records of proceedings
in lists in organisational publications such as annual reports
if it is important to know where an individual works.
A full title is often about using titles in a display or presentation context (display text).
In most contexts, address academics with their full title: title or honorific, name, position, post-nominals and academic institution.

rules.quote: Use full titles in certain contexts
rules.specification: A full title contains the title or honorific, name, applicable post-nominals, position and organisation. For academics the organisation is the academic institution. The page does not define the limits of ‘most contexts’ when addressing academics. Ordinary first and subsequent mentions in body text have their own rules. Post-nominal content and formatting should be checked under the more specific post-nominal rules rather than producing a second finding for the same omission.
rules.violation_condition: An individual is presented without the identifying elements of a full title in a context that calls for a full title.
when: Introducing an individual as a speaker.
Address and signature blocks in correspondence.
Official records of proceedings.
Lists in organisational publications, including annual reports.
Where the individual’s workplace is important.
As the default when addressing academics in most contexts.
rules.why: G-2 and G-4: the listed contexts and academic-address guidance change when the full-title check applies.

covers.quote: To ensure your content is readable, write the title in full.
Shortened forms are sometimes necessary because of limited space. For example, shortened forms often appear in tables.
‘Dr’ is an exception in all instances.
Never use the shortened form of the title in body text (‘Prof’ for example), except for the contraction ‘Dr’.
Some academic titles have an accepted abbreviated title you can use after the first mention.

parts.quote: Departmental officers recently attended Upsilon University’s annual Copyright Symposium. The academic panel (pictured below), chaired by Vice-Chancellor Tom Dhillon, discussed recent cases with implications for fair dealing provisions of the Copyright Act 1968.
Left to right: Associate Professor Sara Baird, Vice-Chancellor Tom Dhillon, Dean Frank Ealing, Adjunct Professor Olena Iraklidis, Dr Celia Nieminen
Left to right: Assoc Prof S Baird, VC T Dhillon, Dean F Ealing, Adj Prof O Iraklidis, Dr C Nieminen
This year’s graduate cohort asked Deputy Vice-Chancellor Jonquil Johansson to moderate their debate.
DVC Jonquil Johansson to moderate their debate.

rules.quote: Only use shortened forms of titles in limited circumstances.
rules.specification: The general rule leaves ‘limited circumstances’ open, with limited space as an explicit example. The body-text restriction is categorical: the page says ‘Never’. An accepted abbreviated academic rank, such as ‘Professor’ for ‘Emeritus Professor’ on subsequent mention, is not the same as a contraction or initialism such as ‘Prof’ or ‘PVC’.
rules.violation_condition: An academic or professional title other than ‘Dr’ is shortened in body text, or is shortened elsewhere without a limited-circumstances justification.
when: Applies to shortened titles immediately before a name.
Limited space can justify shortened forms outside body text, including in tables and image captions.
Body text must use the full form except for ‘Dr’.
‘Dr’ is an exception in all instances.
rules.why: G-2 and G-3: body text, limited space and ‘Dr’ are conditions or exceptions to the same shortened-title check.

covers.quote: People might understand common contractions like ‘Prof’ for ‘Professor’, but some shortened forms are confusing. For example, the initialism for ‘Pro Vice-Chancellor’ is ‘PVC’.

rules.quote: List the full form of any title that people might find confusing in a note.
rules.specification: The page gives no closed list or audience test for confusing shortened titles. A checker needs an audience-sensitive allowlist or reviewer judgement; it should not treat every shortened title as confusing.
rules.violation_condition: A potentially confusing shortened title appears without a note giving its full form.
when: A shortened title is used in circumstances where shortening is otherwise allowed.
The shortened title may confuse the intended audience.
rules.why: This requires a distinct textual element—a note—rather than merely restating the preference for full titles.

Left to right: Assoc Prof S Baird, VC T Dhillon, Dean F Ealing, Adj Prof O Iraklidis, Dr C Nieminen

rules.quote: The space available for image captions can be limited, but write the full names and titles as a default.
rules.specification: This finding concerns shortened personal names. Shortened titles are covered by the general shortened-title rule, avoiding two findings for the same title. Whether space requires initials needs publication-layout information not supplied by the words alone.
rules.violation_condition: An image caption uses personal initials instead of full names when space does not require shortening.
when: Applies to image captions identifying people.
Initials are allowed when limited caption space makes them necessary.
rules.why: G-3: limited space relaxes the full-name default; the permitted shortened caption is not a violating example.

rules.quote: If you have to use initials and the shortened forms of titles in a caption, always include the full forms in body text to provide context.
rules.violation_condition: A caption uses personal initials or shortened titles without the corresponding full forms appearing in body text.
when: A caption uses shortened names or titles because space is limited.
The universal ‘Dr’ exception does not require expansion to ‘Doctor’.
rules.why: This is a separate document-level expansion requirement, not another prohibition on shortened captions.

covers.quote: Use title, name and post-nominals at first mention
The first time you write a name in body text, use the academic and professional title along with the first and last name. Include the post-nominal for a civil or military honour in the title.

parts.quote: Emeritus Professor Stephen Duckett has extensive experience in health care at senior leadership level. Professor Duckett’s membership of the RMIT Council concludes in 2022.
Dr Ziggy Switkowski AO has been chancellor of RMIT since 2011. Dr Switkowski is also chair of NBN Co.

rules.quote: The first time you mention someone in body text, use their academic or professional title before their first name and last name, followed by post-nominals.
rules.violation_condition: The first body-text mention of an individual omits their academic or professional title, first name, last name or applicable civil or military honour post-nominals, or places the title after the personal name.
when: Applies at the first mention in body text.
Post-nominals for civil or military honours are included when applicable.
Academic and professional qualification post-nominals are subject to the separate context restrictions.
‘Dr’ is allowed without being spelt out.
rules.why: G-4: the later post-nominal section restates and qualifies the same first-mention format.

covers.quote: Use post-nominals at first mention only
If you mention the name again, use the title and last name, but don’t include the post-nominal.
Some academic titles have an accepted abbreviated title you can use after the first mention.
[‘Professor’ is the accepted abbreviated title for an Emeritus or Emerita Professor.]

parts.quote: Emeritus Professor Stephen Duckett has extensive experience in health care at senior leadership level. Professor Duckett’s membership of the RMIT Council concludes in 2022.
Dr Ziggy Switkowski AO has been chancellor of RMIT since 2011. Dr Switkowski is also chair of NBN Co.

rules.quote: If you mention the individual again, only use the title and last name.
rules.violation_condition: A subsequent body-text name reference does not use the title and last name alone, for example by repeating given names or post-nominals or dropping the title.
when: Applies to subsequent name mentions in body text, not repeated display titles or correspondence blocks.
An accepted abbreviated academic rank may replace the original rank after first mention.
‘Professor’ is an accepted abbreviated title for an Emeritus or Emerita Professor.
rules.why: G-2 to G-4: omission of post-nominals and accepted abbreviated ranks are parts or exceptions of the subsequent-mention format.

covers.quote: Post-nominals are letters after a name that stand for academic, civil and military awards and honours.

parts.quote: Professor Sally Wheeler OBE MRIA FAcSS FAAL

rules.quote: Write post-nominals after the name in academic and professional titles
rules.violation_condition: Post-nominal letters are placed before the person’s name rather than after it.
when: Post-nominals are included in an academic or professional title.
rules.why: The heading states an independently checkable placement rule, not merely a grouping of its child sections.

covers.quote: Write the post-nominals for the knighthood after the name, followed by any other post-nominals.

parts.quote: Professor Sally Wheeler OBE MRIA FAcSS FAAL

rules.quote: Make sure you write post-nominals in the right order.
rules.specification: The page does not supply a complete precedence order. It specifically says to place knighthood post-nominals before other post-nominals for a knighted doctorate holder, but its Dame Bridget Ogilvie example places AC before DBE. An authoritative ordering source and resolution of this inconsistency are needed; no ordering table should be invented.
rules.violation_condition: A sequence of post-nominals is not in the applicable order of precedence.
when: A person has multiple post-nominals.
The knighted-doctorate subsection states that knighthood post-nominals come before other post-nominals.
rules.why: G-2: the knighted-doctorate instruction is a specific ordering case; the unresolved ordering is made explicit rather than guessed.

covers.quote: Don’t insert commas before or between the post-nominals.

anchor.quote: For Australian correspondence, write ‘Dear Associate Professor’ and ‘Dear Assistant Professor’ not ‘Dear Doctor’ or ‘Dear Professor’.

covers.quote: How to address associate and assistant professors correctly in correspondence differs by country and educational institution.

tags.violation_condition: Australian correspondence addresses an associate or assistant professor as ‘Dear Doctor’ or ‘Dear Professor’, or otherwise substitutes a shortened rank for the specified salutation.

when: Applies to Australian correspondence to an associate professor or assistant professor.
The addressee’s actual academic rank must be known.
rules.why: G-4: the body after the example labels states a new, independently checkable rule.

anchor.quote: When writing ‘Dear’ without the person’s name in emails and letters, write the title ‘Doctor’ in full.

covers.quote: Today, it is acceptable to use ‘Dear Dr Name’ for both formal and informal correspondence.

tags.violation_condition: A nameless email or letter salutation uses ‘Dear Dr’ instead of ‘Dear Doctor’.

when: Applies to emails and letters addressing a person with a doctorate.
The salutation has ‘Dear’ and the title but no personal name.
With a name, ‘Dear Dr Name’ is allowed in formal and informal correspondence.

anchor.quote: If the holder of a doctorate is knighted, don’t address them as ‘Doctor’.

covers.quote: Instead, address the person by ‘Sir’ or ‘Dame’.

tags.violation_condition: A knighted doctorate holder is addressed using the doctorate-based honorific ‘Doctor’ or ‘Dr’ instead of ‘Sir’ or ‘Dame’.

when: The individual holds a doctorate and is knighted.
Applies to the doctorate-based form of address.
rules.why: G-2 and G-4: the prohibition and its positive replacement state one honorific-selection rule.

anchor.quote: Use ‘Doctor’ or ‘Dr’ for medical practitioners, dentists and veterinarians, whether or not they hold a doctorate.
